title: Chinese Tech Giants Order $35 Billion Of Nvidia's Latest 'Compliant' GPUs - Except There's A Huge Problem
desc:
Chinese Tech Giants Order $35 Billion Of Nvidia's Latest 'Compliant' GPUs - Except There's A Huge Problem

ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent have ordered more than 3 million of Nvidia's new RTX PRO 5500 workstation GPUs, representing a collective sticker price exceeding $35 billion, as Chinese tech giants scramble for export-compliant hardware amid ongoing U.S. trade restrictions, Reuters reported Tuesday, citing sources familiar with the matter.

Nvidia has warned customers and partners that it cannot guarantee fulfillment because Chinese demand vastly outstrips planned production. One source indicated that buyers were informed they might receive only 5% to 10% of their requested quantities, while another noted the company expects to produce no more than 3 million RTX PRO 5500 cards globally throughout 2027. Total orders from Chinese customers alone have already surpassed 6 million units, according to the sources. The three tech giants are seeking cards priced at approximately $11,400 each, with Nvidia advising customers to expect early samples in December and commercial deliveries to begin in the first quarter of 2027.

The RTX PRO 5500 is a Blackwell-architecture workstation GPU engineered for high-performance professional systems rather than massive data-center clusters. Built on the same GB202 die as the GeForce RTX 5090, it features roughly 21,760 CUDA cores, 84 GB of GDDR7 ECC memory, and about 1,398 GB/s of bandwidth. Chinese firms primarily intend to deploy the cards for AI inference - running trained models to process chatbot responses and other user-facing tasks - rather than the heavier training workloads restricted to Nvidia's premier data-center accelerators.

Under current U.S. export controls, Nvidia's most advanced Blackwell data-center processors, such as the B300, are barred from sale to Chinese buyers, while shipments of the older Hopper-based H200 face case-by-case licensing reviews. Consequently, the RTX PRO 5500 stands among the most powerful Nvidia chips legally available to the Chinese market under existing regulations.

The massive order volume highlights the enduring demand for Nvidia hardware among Chinese technology enterprises despite years of tightening U.S. export policies. As Reuters noted last month, China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology previously directed firms like ByteDance and Alibaba to report their procurement plans for the RTX PRO 5500, signaling intended government approval. That followed reports that ByteDance alone was weighing an order of roughly one million units.

China is weighing allowing domestic companies to buy $NVDA new RTX Pro 5500 with ByteDance reportedly considering an order of ~1 million chips as local AI demand outruns supply.

Nvidia says Chinese chipmakers have seen "unprecedented growth since 2022" so even a partial reopening could give it a path back into a market where its AI share fell from like 95% to nearly zero.

— Shay Boloor (@StockSavvyShay) September 27, 2026

This dynamic reflects a familiar pattern. Successive export controls have severely eroded Nvidia's historical dominance in China's AI data-center chip market. Earlier compliance-focused products, including the H20 and the RTX 6000D, encountered regulatory friction, production bottlenecks, or eventual discontinuation; secondary-market prices for the pulled RTX 6000D have roughly doubled in China, according to Reuters sources. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has previously noted that U.S. trade restrictions reduced the company's share of China's AI data-center accelerator market to a fraction of its former scale.

Concurrently, export limitations have created an opening for domestic alternatives. Huawei and other local semiconductor firms have steadily gained ground with native AI accelerators, even as Chinese tech giants continue to chase any accessible Nvidia silicon. The $35 billion figure represents total requested sticker-price value rather than confirmed revenue; actual deliveries will represent only a fraction of those volumes due to strict manufacturing limits and Nvidia's ongoing reallocation of TSMC production capacity toward its next-generation Rubin platform for 2027.

Whether Beijing ultimately grants final approval for the full scale of imports, and how many units Nvidia can successfully deliver, remains uncertain. For now, the reported order surge demonstrates that Chinese hyperscalers remain deeply committed to Nvidia's software ecosystem for inference workloads - even when forced down to workstation-class hardware - highlighting the enduring tension between geopolitical export controls and global market demand.

title: Trump Unveils $8 Billion Harvest Fuel Relief Program To Support Farmers
desc:
Trump Unveils $8 Billion Harvest Fuel Relief Program To Support Farmers

Authored by Travis Gillmore via The Epoch Times,

President Donald Trump announced a new Department of Agriculture program offering $8 billion to farmers during harvest season, as rising diesel costs strain operations nationwide.

"And when the Republicans win, we will pass even more funding for our farmers," Trump told a standing-room-only crowd of thousands during a rally in the Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City, just north of Wichita, Kansas.

The Harvest Fuel Relief program will use a formula to determine losses and offset increased diesel costs, with calculations similar to those used in the established Farmer Bridge Assistance program, according to a statement from the Department of Agriculture.

Farmer Cliff Carter works on an irrigation system for one of his rice fields in Rector, Ark., on June 5, 2026. Karen Pulfer Focht/Reuters

"This $8 billion dollar investment will help bring certainty to our farmers during this harvest so they can continue to feed our nation," Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said in a statement released shortly after the president's announcement.

Diesel prices averaged $6.18 per gallon nationwide as of Oct. 12, up about $2.51 per gallon from the same time last year, according to the most recent data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

During an approximately 90-minute address, Trump highlighted recent policies his administration enacted to benefit farmers and rural Americans, including raising production targets for ethanol-based biofuels to the highest levels recorded, a move the president estimated would boost farm incomes in Kansas by $4 billion, collectively, per year.

He noted a recently signed waiver allowing the year-round sale of E15 gasoline could become permanent, but only if Republicans win in the upcoming midterm elections.

"If you want to see what is at stake in this election, just look at what's happening in France, a once-great nation that is being conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists who hate Christianity, and they hate, frankly, the Western civilization itself," Trump said.

"Americans are going to stand up and declare that we will defend our culture, we will protect our civilization, we will preserve our religion, our values, and our heritage, and we will never let our nation be conquered or destroyed by people that hate us."

President Donald Trump reacts during a rally in support of Republican U.S. Senate reelection candidate Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) in Park City, Kan., on Oct. 19, 2026. Jonathan Ernst/Reuters

Incumbent first-term Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, facing Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton in a race recent polls suggest is a toss-up, told the crowd his reelection would support "secure borders, a strong military, and lower taxes."

A loss would potentially allow Democrats to gain a majority and overtake consequential Senate committee positions, he said.

"If Kansas loses this Senate race, Chuck Schumer will control the Senate. Elizabeth Warren would control the Bank Committee, and Bernie Sanders would control the Health Care Committee, and Cory Booker, a vegan, would control the [Agriculture] Committee," Marshall said.

"We need a senator on the ag committee that can sort heifers and steers, not someone who doesn't know the difference between a bull and a steer."

Hamilton co-founded the United Methodist Church of the Resurrection in Leawood, Kansas, and supported the inclusion of same-sex marriages and other changes to church protocols that led to division among some congregations.

His campaign is focused on reducing the cost of living and changing rules for elected officials, including establishing term-limits and blocking Congress members and their families from trading stocks.

"Washington has become overrun by chaos and corruption, with far too many politicians on both sides of the aisle putting themselves and special interests first instead of listening to their constituents' needs. It's time for a change," Hamilton said in a statement, citing "rampant conflicts of interest and self-dealing," among other issues he aims to correct.

"Kansans deserve leaders who truly believe in government ethics and real accountability."

Republican nominee for governor Ty Masterson is running against Democrat state Sen. Cindy Holscher to replace term-limited Democrat Laura Kelly.

"This isn't about any individual running for an elected office, myself included," Masterson said during the rally. "It's about the future of this state and this country. It's about the next generation."

The candidate reiterated a common theme of recent rallies, that those in attendance are the catalyst for a Republican victory if they mobilize their networks.

"You must get out and vote, and you must bring 10 of your friends because the stakes are that high, they really are," Masterson said.

Rocker Ted Nugent boosted the energy in the arena with a surprise appearance, telling the audience his "life pivots upon God, family, country, Constitution, the Bill of Rights, the 10 Commandments, the Golden Rule, work ethic, law and order, self-defense, [and] private property rights."

He commended the veterans in attendance and those around the world who served and those on duty defending the country.

"Politics is we the people thanking those flag-draped coffins for their sacrifice by voting for the beliefs they died for," Nugent said.

"You've always seen me rock and roll on stage, but I've always stood up for the truth, logic, and common sense, the God-given individual freedoms that they died for that is guaranteed in that sacred United States Constitution."

The president's visit to Kansas marked his first in the state since a Topeka rally in 2018. He is in the midst of a midterm blitz to support Republican candidates, having rallied in Kentucky, Georgia, Montana, Ohio, and New York in recent days, with stops in North Carolina, South Carolina, Iowa, Florida, and another Georgia rally on the schedule, with more expected through Nov. 3.

title: US Pending Home Sales Collapse To Record Lows In September
desc:
US Pending Home Sales Collapse To Record Lows In September

And the housing market's annus horribilis continues (existing home sales near COVID lows, mortgage rates at three year highs, homebuilder confidence at GFC lows, homebuyer confidence at record lows, housing starts near COVID lows)...

After a very small rebound (+0.3% MoM) in August, US Pending Home Sales collapsed (-7.3% MoM vs -3.9% MoM exp) in September. That dragged

“Market conditions weakened in September due to fast-rising mortgage rates,” says Lawrence Yun, NAR’s chief economist.

“Although job growth and income gains can support home purchases, housing affordability is more affected by changes in mortgage rates...

...Buyers and sellers may simply be holding back until mortgage rates move favorably.”

September's slump smashes the Pending Home Sales Index to a record low...

But Yun believes - ever the optimist - that the rapid run-up in mortgage rates over the last month may be nearing the end.

“Given that mortgage rates have already risen much more than the Federal Reserve’s short-term interest rate hikes, mortgage rates could be topping out,” Yun says.

“However, increasing energy prices and the resulting inflationary pressures are highly uncertain.”

For the week of October 11, the 30-year fixed mortgage rate came in at 7.40% per Freddie Mac, flat sequentially and up 113bps YOY. Mortgage applications fell 37% YOY along with refinancings down 56% YOY, both similar to last week, while purchase volumes declined 16% YOY vs -15% last week. ARMs accounted for 11% of volume, up 20bps sequentially and vs 9% last year. Purchase applications were down 4% sequentially as rates hold at a 52-week high, though they are 5% above the February 2025 trough.

Goldman Sachs economists sum things up succinctly: "We expect near-term [housing] activity to remain under pressure given the rate and broader macro backdrop."

Contract signings in September dropped by the largest percentage in the West, falling 9.2% from August and down 15% from a year ago. The South followed with an 8.2% month-over-month and 12% annual decrease in September. The Midwest posted a 6.5% monthly decline and 8.7% decrease from a year ago.

Meanwhile, the Northeast fared best, but with pending home sales still falling 4.2% in September compared to August and down 9.4% from a year earlier. title: US Ambassador Warns EU Of 'Devastating' Retaliation Over Tech Restrictions
desc:
US Ambassador Warns EU Of 'Devastating' Retaliation Over Tech Restrictions

Authored by Owen Evans via The Epoch Times,

European companies could face "devastating" retaliation from Washington if Brussels restricts American tech rivals, the U.S. ambassador to the European Union said on Oct 19.

Ambassador Andrew Puzder told the Financial Times that European businesses should be wary of possible retaliatory measures, given the size of the U.S. market.

Puzder questioned whether restricting American competition would improve the competitiveness of European companies.

"If the purpose is to make the United States less competitive, I think that that's not a legitimate goal," he told the FT.

"You don't make European companies more competitive by making U.S. companies less competitive.

"We have best-in-class products in this area. They're reliable products, they're trusted products. We don't need some kind of synchronised mediocrity."

The European Commission is pushing for technological sovereignty.

It proposed new rules in May for allocating the 2 GHz frequency band, which supports satellite communications and emerging services allowing mobile phones to connect directly to satellites.

It does not explicitly propose banning SpaceX or all American operators.

On Oct. 19, four European telecommunications companies - Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefónica, and Vodafone - announced that they had signed a letter of intent to explore a joint bid for European satellite spectrum.

The ambassador also questioned the motive behind the EU's enforcement of its Digital Markets Act (DMA).

"You start to wonder, are we trying to deal with the competition in the digital marketplace or are we trying to generate revenue from American companies to benefit Europe?" he said.

The DMA regulates large digital gatekeepers, including American companies such as Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta Platforms, and Microsoft.

Separately, the Digital Services Act (DSA) requires major online platforms to address illegal content and certain systemic risks.

Last month, French European Affairs Minister Benjamin Haddad suggested that proceeds from fines imposed on Google should reduce member states' contributions to the EU budget.

"This is a new revenue source for the European Union - worth €4.6 billion - that should automatically lower the contributions of all member states," Haddad told Franceinfo on Sept. 29.

The ambassador urged Europe "to let go of this regulatory mindset where they're going to try and stop things because we're in a race with China" both on AI and on quantum computing.

He added the U.S. can win that race, "but it'd be a lot easier if we were working with Europe instead of fighting Europe."

The Epoch Times contacted the EU Commission for comment.

Ukraine and Starlink

The transatlantic dispute comes amid a separate issue over restrictions on SpaceX's Starshield satellite communications system used by Ukraine's military.

Starlink supports battlefield communications and drones used to attack Russian targets.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed in an Oct. 18 interview that a restriction on Starlink satellite internet that disrupted Ukrainian combat missions and threatened defenses against Russian drones for three days was a "message" from America's government.

Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy, said on Oct. 14 that the restrictions affected terminals using the Starshield military service package when traveling faster than 100 mph.

Ukraine's defense forces received no advance notice, he said, and several missions were disrupted.

British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting confirmed on Oct. 15 that Ukraine's access to SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield services had been restored following a temporary disruption.

Following a meeting with U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth on Oct. 15, Streeting told the BBC that he was "reassured directly" by Hegseth that Ukraine's access to Starlink and Starshield had been restored.

On Sunday, Zelenskyy said that the United States has resumed its sharing of important intelligence with Ukraine to help defend the country against Russia.

Separately, on Oct. 19, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied Zelenskyy's assertion that U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukraine had temporarily been suspended.

"There's been no pause," Rubio told reporters during a visit to Uzbekistan.

title: General Motors Shares Plunge 6% Despite $20 Billion Buyback Announcement And Earnings Beat
desc:
General Motors Shares Plunge 6% Despite $20 Billion Buyback Announcement And Earnings Beat

General Motors shares are plunging more than 6% in premarket trading Tuesday, despite the automaker announcing a massive new $20 billion share repurchase program and reporting quarterly earnings that came in ahead of Wall Street expectations, according to Bloomberg News.

The selling comes as GM continues to grapple with a weakening U.S. auto market, where higher financing costs and pressure on household budgets have made it increasingly difficult to sell lower-priced vehicles. Demand for the company's more expensive trucks and SUVs has held up considerably better, allowing GM to preserve profitability even as overall sales volumes come under pressure.

Bloomberg/Financial Post reports that for the third quarter, GM generated approximately $50 billion in revenue and $4.1 billion in adjusted operating profit, narrowly beating analyst expectations. Adjusted earnings of $3.70 per share also exceeded the $3.56 consensus estimate. Perhaps more importantly, automotive free cash flow jumped 40% to $5.9 billion.

That cash generation is helping fund an increasingly aggressive effort to return money to shareholders. GM's latest $20 billion repurchase authorization follows a $6 billion program announced earlier this year and approximately $29.5 billion in buybacks completed since 2023. The newest authorization is expected to be used over several years.

Management also tightened its 2026 earnings forecast, now expecting adjusted operating profit between $14.5 billion and $15.5 billion, versus its previous projection of $14 billion to $16 billion. The midpoint of the guidance remains unchanged.

Looking ahead, GM is putting additional emphasis on its bread-and-butter pickup business, with redesigned Chevrolet Silverado and GMC Sierra trucks expected later this year. The company also plans to increase output of higher-end models equipped with V-8 engines, betting that wealthier consumers will continue paying a premium for larger vehicles.

The approach marks a notable change from GM's previous enthusiasm for electric vehicles and autonomous driving, both of which have resulted in expensive setbacks. CEO Mary Barra has increasingly redirected attention toward established profit centers, while pursuing more targeted opportunities in vehicle software, advanced driver assistance and even defense-related manufacturing.

GM's overseas operations, meanwhile, continue to struggle. Quarterly profit from China fell 60% from a year earlier to just $32 million.

The broader auto industry has undergone a significant reassessment over the past two years. After spending much of the early 2020s promising an accelerated transition to electric vehicles, several major manufacturers have scaled back EV investments, delayed launches and absorbed substantial losses as consumer adoption failed to match earlier expectations.

At the same time, persistently expensive vehicles, elevated interest rates and increasingly stretched consumers have complicated the outlook for traditional auto sales. The result is an industry increasingly focused on protecting margins, generating cash and selling the vehicles customers are actually willing to buy, rather than pursuing the ambitious growth narratives that dominated the sector just a few years ago.

title: EU NatGas Hits 2022 Crisis Levels As Goldman Warns 150 Euros Could Be Next
desc:
EU NatGas Hits 2022 Crisis Levels As Goldman Warns 150 Euros Could Be Next

Back in late August, Goldman Sachs commodities expert Samantha Dart warned that EU natural gas prices would need to soar dramatically to discourage Asian LNG demand and shift cargoes to Europe amid disruptions at the Strait of Hormuz.

*EUROPE'S GAS BENCHMARK EXCEEDS €90 FOR FIRST TIME SINCE 2022

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 20, 2026

Fast forward to Tuesday morning, European gas prices (TTF) have topped 90 euros per megawatt-hour, the highest level since late 2022. Notably, Dart warned about where prices were headed when EU NatGas was trading around 67 euros.

Separately, Goldman's Daan Struyven and Dart released a new note earlier today, putting their base case for Brent crude at $90 a barrel and European benchmark EU NatGas at 70 euros by year-end, assuming a recovery in Middle Eastern supply and easing risk premiums. Brent is forecast to average $80 in 2027.

However, they warned that risks remained skewed toward the upside: Brent crude could climb to $140 early next year and average about $125 in 2027 if Gulf oil output averages 5 million barrels a day below February 2026 levels. As for EU NatGas, they warned it could soar to 150 euros if Gulf LNG exports remain at just one quarter of normal levels and a more severe winter boosts heating demand.

Here's what they said:

Our base case is that a further recovery in Mideast supply and a moderation in the risk premium reduce prices of Brent crude and European natural gas to $90/bbl and EUR70/MWh, respectively, by end-2026.2 However, we remain concerned that geopolitical escalation—such as intensified shipping attacks or damage to energy infrastructure—and, for European natural gas, a cold winter could push energy prices significantly higher.

While estimated Persian Gulf exports of crude oil—including estimated dark exports— remained near their 2025 average over the past 7 days (Exhibit 2), they edged down from the early October highs as attacks on ships attempting to cross Hormuz have picked up (Exhibit 2). Estimated Gulf exports of refined oil products are much lower at around 40% of the 2025 average, in part reflecting Mideast refinery outages. Similarly, visible LNG crossings through Hormuz, have edged down this month relative to late October levels.

Misses in Mideast supply could push energy prices significantly higher:

  • Brent might rally to $140 in early 2027 and average around $125/bbl in 2027 (red line, Exhibit 4) if 2027 average Gulf output remains 5mb/d below Feb26 levels (while refined product prices would likely rise further from already very high levels)
  • TTF might rally to 150 EUR/MWh by year-end if Persian Gulf LNG exports don't improve beyond 25% of normal and if the winter realizes 1 std. dev. colder than average (Exhibit 5)

Beyond energy, the analysts noted that the Bloomberg Commodity Index delivered a 36% total return this year, outperforming equities and bonds.

As ex-Goldman Sachs Jeff Currie, including ourselves, has pointed out, commodities have entered a period of scarcity, whether due to resource nationalism, adverse weather, supply woes, and more.

title: Charles Schwab, JPMorgan Restrict Third-Party AI Agents Over Security Risk
desc:
Charles Schwab, JPMorgan Restrict Third-Party AI Agents Over Security Risk

Authored by Bill Pan via The Epoch Times,

Some of Wall Street's largest financial firms are blocking third-party artificial intelligence agents from directly accessing customer accounts or moving money, citing concerns about security, control, and accountability if an autonomous system makes a mistake.

Charles Schwab, which reported $13.3 trillion in client assets at the end of the third quarter, is one of the latest firms to draw that line.

"We are blocking unauthorized agents who try to log in on behalf of clients," President and CEO Rick Wurster told analysts on Oct. 14 during Schwab's third-quarter earnings call.

The concern is not AI itself, he said, but outside agents using a customer's credentials and operating inside Schwab's systems without controls imposed by the brokerage.

Instead, Schwab plans to give third-party AI models a controlled way to connect via Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.

MCP allows an AI system to interact with outside data and services through defined permissions. Under Schwab's approach, an outside AI model could potentially retrieve information such as account balances or investment research while being blocked from higher-risk actions, including moving money.

Schwab is also rolling out its own generative AI assistant, Charley, which can answer questions and perform certain administrative tasks on customers' behalf.

Schwab is not alone. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has confirmed that the bank will not allow just any outside AI agent into its systems to protect customers and the bank.

"You don't want rogue agents, and there could be thousands of them," Dimon said during an Oct. 13 earnings call.

A "rogue" agent generally refers to an AI system that takes actions outside the boundaries intended by its user or developer while pursuing its assigned goal.

Dimon also warned customers that if they're giving third-party AI agents access to their bank accounts, they're owning that decision.

"There's a liability transfer. They should understand the liability transfer," he said. "If data is being misused, they should understand it's being misused."

Could AI Move Deposits Faster?

Beyond cybersecurity, autonomous AI could also change the economics of banking.

Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Sløk warned in September that increasingly capable financial assistants could eventually create what he called an "agentic bank run."

Unlike a traditional bank run, in which customers withdraw money out of fear that a bank might fail, an agentic bank run could be driven by software that constantly seeks higher returns.

An AI assistant, for example, could continually compare interest rates and automatically move a household's cash from a low-yield checking account into higher-paying alternatives.

Apollo noted that some fintech and online accounts were offering yields ranging from 3.3 percent to 5 percent, compared with a national average of roughly 0.1 percent for checking accounts.

If AI made moving money nearly frictionless, Sløk argued, banks could lose some of the inexpensive deposits they rely on to fund loans.

Not every bank executive believes that prospect is happening any soon.

In an Oct. 13 earnings call, Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf said the idea of an AI-driven exodus to higher-yielding alternatives was "completely overdone."

"High-rate alternatives exist today. They've existed for a long time," Scharf told analysts. "If you want to move to a high rate, you can just go online and do it yourself in no time. That's not something new."

Who Is Liable When an AI Agent Goes Rogue?

Concerns about giving AI systems greater autonomy have been heightened by a series of cybersecurity incidents this year.

In July, ChatGPT developer OpenAI disclosed that a group, or "swarm," of its AI agents had broken out of restrictions within a testing environment and compromised the systems of Hugging Face, an online platform widely used by AI developers.

Separately, OpenAI apologized to the Australian government in September after one of its AI models infiltrated Australian government websites during a training exercise.

There is no single federal law that comprehensively assigns liability between an AI developer, the company deploying the system, and the user when an autonomous agent causes damage. Existing laws may apply depending on the circumstances.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has argued against giving AI developers broad immunity from liability.

"What we shouldn't do on safety is to give these labs a liability exemption, which is what they are asking for," Bessent said while testifying before the House Financial Services Committee on Sept. 15.

"The best way to guarantee safety is that the creators are liable for what they build and generate."

Earlier this month, Sens. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) introduced the bipartisan AI Agent Accountability Act, aimed specifically at hacking carried out by AI agents.

Under the proposal, operators could face civil and criminal liability under federal computer-crime law if they knowingly operate an AI agent that recklessly causes hacking-related damage or loss.

Developers could also be held liable if they knew an agent was capable of hacking but failed to implement reasonable safeguards.

The bill would also allow the U.S. attorney general and state attorneys general to seek court orders against certain AI-agent hacking activity.

title: Saudi Arabia Executes Two Foreigners Over 'Indecent Acts' Inside Mecca Mosque
desc:
Saudi Arabia Executes Two Foreigners Over 'Indecent Acts' Inside Mecca Mosque

Via Middle East Eye

Bangladesh is seeking answers on why Saudi Arabia executed two Bangladeshi nationals in the city of Mecca - which is considered holy in Islam - without telling Dhaka.

Last week, Saudi Arabia executed a male and a female Bangladeshi national after they were convicted of committing "indecent acts" inside a mosque (in Mecca).

Riyadh did not provide further details on the acts the two Bangladeshi nationals allegedly committed or whether they had legal representation in the Gulf kingdom, according to local media reports.

Reacting to the incident, Bangladesh’s minister for foreign affairs, Humaiun Kobir, told reporters that he was "very disappointed" by the lack of communication and that Dhaka was seeking an explanation on why they were executed and not informed beforehand about the execution.

"We have sought an explanation from our friendly bilateral partner to look into the matter and know why the gap in information sharing and exchanges happened here. We are in discussions," he told reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday.

Earlier, the Bangladeshi foreign ministry said that it was waiting for a copy of the full verdict and the circumstances that led to the execution.

The official added that the two executed Bangladeshis were included in a list of prisoners that Saudi Arabia had shared with Bangladesh but did not indicate that they had planned to execute them.

Last week, Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court overturned the death sentence of a Sri Lankan national after he allegedly insulted Islam and the Prophet Muhammad.

Sri Lanka’s Deputy Foreign Minister Arun Hemachandra confirmed that Riyadh had overturned the death sentence of Anojan Sivarasa.

The 27-year-old remains imprisoned after he was sentenced to five years in prison and fined three million Saudi Riyals ($800,000).

The court handed down the sentence amid intense criticism of Riyadh's legal system.

Saudi Arabia relies on interpretations of Islamic law, alongside cybercrime and counterterror legislation, to target online expression under the guise of protecting "public morals".
